title: Why Do Bottle Caps Have Teeth?

fin.small: Sources: W. Painter, US Patent 468,258, 'Bottle-Sealing Device', 2 Feb 1892; Wikipedia, 'Bottle cap' (24 and 21 teeth).

parts: Count the teeth on a metal bottle cap. The standard one has twenty-one.
Stay to the end for what those teeth have to do with your bottle opener.
In 1892, William Painter of Baltimore patented a metal cap for bottles.
Glass necks back then were never quite the same width.
So he folded the cap's edge into ridges, like a tiny accordion.
His patent says the ridges let one cap fit bottles of different widths.
No. His first caps had twenty-four. Today's standard is twenty-one.
Why the change? We found no engineering test that settles it.
And the opener? The same patent says each ridge leaves an edge for an opener to hook. He was planning it already.
Our reading: those teeth aren't decoration. They hold the seal on and give your opener its grip. Subscribe for the next one.
